questions.subtopic: 5.17 The area between a sideways parabola and a chord, integrated with respect to y
tags: region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis
questions.challenge_mechanism: The region is perfectly ordinary and the integral that measures it is easy, but only if the candidate integrates with respect to y, which means treating x as the dependent variable. The curve is given as x = y^2 and the boundary as x = 3 - 2y, so the region is described naturally by horizontal strips and the single integral runs from y = -3 to y = 1. A candidate who insists on vertical strips has to notice that the top of the region is the upper branch of the parabola for part of its width and the straight line for the rest, so the integral splits in two at x = 1 and the second half needs a square root. The problem has not changed difficulty, it has changed coordinate, and the item is built so that the awkward version is the one the candidate will reach for by habit. The figure marks the split point on the diagram so that the two descriptions can be compared rather than argued about.
questions.question:
The region $R$ is enclosed by the curve $x = y^{2}$ and the straight line $x = 3 - 2y$, as shown in the figure. The two boundary curves meet at $(9,\,-3)$ and at $(1,\,1)$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the two points at which the curve and the line meet, by forming and solving an equation in $y$.

(b) Show that the area of $R$ is given by the single integral $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{1}\left(3 - 2y - y^{2}\right)dy$ and evaluate it.

(c) Explain why integrating with respect to $x$ instead would require the region to be split into two parts, and state the value of $x$ at which the split would occur.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the two points at which the curve $x = y^{2}$ and the line $x = 3 - 2y$ meet, by forming and solving an equation in $y$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the region $R$ is given by $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{1}\left(3 - 2y - y^{2}\right)dy$, and evaluate this integral.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why integrating with respect to $x$ instead of $y$ would require the region to be split into two parts, and state the value of $x$ at which the split would occur.

questions.answer:
**(a)** A point on both curves satisfies $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$, so $y^{2} + 2y - 3 = 0$ (M1). Factorising, $(y + 3)(y - 1) = 0$, so $y = -3$ or $y = 1$. Substituting back gives $x = y^{2} = 9$ when $y = -3$ and $x = 1$ when $y = 1$, so the two points are $(9,\,-3)$ and $(1,\,1)$ (A1).

**(b)** For every $y$ between $-3$ and $1$ the line lies to the right of the curve, because $3 - 2y - y^{2} = -(y + 3)(y - 1)$ is positive on that interval (M1). A horizontal strip at height $y$ therefore has width $(3 - 2y) - y^{2}$ and height $dy$, and the area of $R$ is the sum of those strips:

$$A = \int_{-3}^{1}\left(3 - 2y - y^{2}\right)dy = \left[3y - y^{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}y^{3}\right]_{-3}^{1} \;(M1).$$

At the upper limit, $3 - 1 - \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{5}{3}$. At the lower limit, $-9 - 9 + 9 = -9$. Subtracting,

$$A = \tfrac{5}{3} - (-9) = \tfrac{32}{3} \approx 10.67 \;(A1).$$

So the enclosed area is $\tfrac{32}{3}$ square units, which is a little over ten and a half. Notice that the antiderivative is a cubic whose value at the lower limit is negative: the region straddles the $x$-axis, and the integral handles that without any adjustment because the strips are measured horizontally and each one keeps its own sign of $x$, not of $y$.

**(c)** Integrating with respect to $x$ means slicing the region vertically, and the top of a vertical slice is not the same curve all the way across (M1). To the left of the point where the two boundaries cross, the slice runs from the lower branch of the parabola to the upper branch, so its height is $2\sqrt{x}$; to the right of that point the upper branch of the parabola lies above the line, so the height becomes $\dfrac{3 - x}{2} + \sqrt{x}$ and the two curves have exchanged roles as the upper boundary. The change happens where $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$ has its positive root, that is at $y = 1$, and there $x = 1$; this is the dashed vertical line drawn in the figure, and it is the only vertical slice for which the two descriptions agree, since it runs from $y = -1$ to $y = 1$ (A1). A candidate working in $x$ must therefore write

$$A = \int_{0}^{1} 2\sqrt{x}\,dx + \int_{1}^{9}\left(\frac{3 - x}{2} + \sqrt{x}\right)dx = \tfrac{4}{3} + \tfrac{28}{3} = \tfrac{32}{3},$$

which is the same area at roughly twice the work: two integrals, two antiderivatives, and a split point that has to be found before either integral can be set up. Investing in the coordinate that matches the shape of the region is what removes the split.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for forming $y^{2} = 3 - 2y$ or the equivalent and reducing it to $y^{2} + 2y - 3 = 0$; (A1) for both points $(9,\,-3)$ and $(1,\,1)$ with the substitution shown. Accept a candidate who solves for $x$ first, provided both coordinates of both points are stated. A candidate who gives the roots $y = -3$ and $y = 1$ but never forms the coordinates scores the first mark only.

(b) (M1) for setting up the integral with the line minus the curve over $y$ from $-3$ to $1$, with the sign of $3 - 2y - y^{2}$ justified or evidently checked; (M1) for the correct antiderivative $3y - y^{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}y^{3}$; (A1) for $\tfrac{32}{3}$ or $10.7$ to three significant figures. Three fields; credit two, and the displayed integral already earns the first. Do not accept an area given as negative, and do not accept $\tfrac{27}{3}$ or $9$ from substituting the limits in the wrong order.

(c) (M1) for the observation that the upper boundary changes from the upper branch of the parabola to the straight line; (A1) for $x = 1$, correctly located as the point where the interval of $y$ is the largest. Award the second mark for $x = 1$ alone, but only if the change of upper boundary has been stated. A candidate who says the region must be split 'because it is curved' has not identified what changes and scores nothing.
questions.explanation:
The mathematics here is a single quadratic and a single cubic. What the item tests is whether the candidate chooses the variable that the shape of the region is built for, and it is written so that the wrong choice is also the habitual one. Curves are almost always presented as $y$ equal to something in $x$, and the area between two of them is almost always computed with vertical strips, so the reflex is to make $y$ the subject and integrate in $x$ -- which here means solving $x = y^{2}$ for $y$, meeting the square root, and then discovering that the upper boundary is a different curve over part of the range.

Reading the figure instead of the algebra gives the answer immediately. The region is tall and narrow towards its right-hand end and pinches to a point at its left-hand end, and both of its boundaries are naturally described with $y$ as the running variable: one is $x$ as a function of $y$ and the other is $x$ as a function of $y$. Horizontal strips therefore run from one boundary to the other over the whole height of the region, from $y = -3$ to $y = 1$, and one integral does the whole job. The split at $x = 1$ is not a complication of the region; it is a complication created by the choice of coordinate.

It is worth noticing what the single integral does not have to do. There is no square root in it, because the curve is already written as $x$ in terms of $y$. There is no sign correction, even though the region lies mostly below the $x$-axis, because horizontal strips measure differences in $x$ and the question of whether a strip is above or below the axis never arises. And there is no need to find the maximum of anything, because the widest part of the region is at $y = -1$ and no part of the work depends on it.

The general lesson is the one the syllabus states and the exercises rarely enforce: the area of a region can be found by integrating with respect to either variable, and the useful skill is deciding which one keeps the region in a single piece. A region bounded on one side by a curve written as $x$ equal to a function of $y$ is asking to be cut into horizontal strips, and taking the hint is not a trick, it is reading the question.

provenance.adaptation: Written for AHL 5.17, which covers the area of a region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis. The region here is bounded by a parabola given as x in terms of y and by a chord, so the area follows from a single integral in y while the same region in x needs a split at x = 1, and part (c) asks for the split to be located and explained. Both boundaries, both intersection points and the value 32/3 were chosen so that the two formulations produce the same rational answer, which lets the candidate check the coordinate choice rather than take it on trust.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the curve as a function of x, solve x = y^2 for y to get y equal to plus or minus the square root of x, and set up the area as an integral in x between the lower and upper branches, scanning x from 0 to 9.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Treating x as the independent variable is what makes the region two pieces rather than one, because the upper boundary of a vertical slice is the upper branch of the parabola only up to x = 1 and the straight line after it. The region is described without any square root or split if y is made the independent variable, so the difficulty is created by the choice of coordinate and removed by exchanging it.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The area is computed as a single integral from x = 0 to x = 9 of twice the square root of x, which gives 4/3 + 28/3 replaced by 36, an answer more than three times too large, or the integral is abandoned as requiring a split that the candidate then cannot set up.

verification.method: The two intersections were found by solving the quadratic in y and confirmed by substituting the roots into both boundary equations. The single integral in y was evaluated symbolically and numerically, giving 32/3. The split formulation was evaluated independently as the sum of two integrals in x, four thirds plus twenty-eight thirds, which reproduces 32/3 and confirms the location of the split at x = 1. The difference of the two boundary functions was checked to be positive at six interior values of y.
solution_skeleton: Solve y^2 = 3 - 2y to get y = -3 and y = 1, and substitute for the two points.
Check that 3 - 2y - y^2 is positive between the roots, so the line is the right-hand boundary.
Integrate 3 - 2y - y^2 from -3 to 1 and evaluate the cubic at both limits.
Identify x = 1 as the vertical line where the upper boundary changes.
Recompute the area as the sum of two integrals in x and confirm 32/3.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 5.11 Definite integrals, including the analytical approach; SL 5.10 Indefinite integral of x to the power n (n rational); AHL 5.13 The evaluation of limits
questions.subtopic: 5.11 Two unbounded regions, one of which encloses a finite area, decided by the exponent
questions.challenge_mechanism: The two panels look like the same kind of object. Both curves fall towards the axis, both regions run to infinity to the right, and nothing in the picture announces that one of them settles at an area of exactly 1 while the other has no area at all. The question is settled by the antiderivative and by the sign of its exponent: integrating x to the power minus p gives x to the power one minus p, so the behaviour at the upper limit depends on whether that exponent is negative or positive, which is the same as asking whether p exceeds 1. A candidate who reasons from the picture, or who measures the width of the region instead of the height of the curve, expects both tails to be infinite and is surprised by one of them. The second panel is made only four times flatter than the first in the sense that matters, so the difference has to be traced to the exponent rather than to any gross feature of the graphs.
questions.question:
The figure shows the graphs of $y = \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ for $x \geq 1$. In each panel the region between the curve and the $x$-axis, from $x = 1$ onwards, is shaded. Both shaded regions extend without limit to the right.

(a) Show that the area of the region under $y = \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ between $x = 1$ and $x = t$ is $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$, and hence state the area of the shaded region in the left-hand panel.

(b) Show that the area of the region under $y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ between $x = 1$ and $x = t$ is $2\sqrt{t} - 2$, and explain what this shows about the shaded region in the right-hand panel.

(c) Both shaded regions are unbounded in extent. Explain, using the two antiderivatives you have found, which property of the integrand decides whether such a region has a finite area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area of the region under $y = \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ between $x = 1$ and $x = t$ is $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$, and state the area of the shaded region in the left-hand panel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the region under $y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ between $x = 1$ and $x = t$ is $2\sqrt{t} - 2$, and explain what this shows about the shaded region in the right-hand panel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, using the two antiderivatives you have found, which property of the integrand decides whether an unbounded region of this kind has a finite area.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Writing $x^{-2}$ and integrating, $$\int_{1}^{t} x^{-2}\,dx = \left[-x^{-1}\right]_{1}^{t} = -\frac{1}{t} + 1 = 1 - \frac{1}{t} \;(M1)(A1).$$

As $t$ increases without bound the term $\dfrac{1}{t}$ tends to $0$, so the partial area increases towards the value $1$. The shaded region is unbounded in extent but encloses exactly one square unit: to reach an area of $0.99$ the region must be extended to $t = 100$, to reach $0.999$ to $t = 1000$, and no finite $t$ ever achieves the full unit (A1). Each doubling of the extent adds less than half of what the previous doubling added, and the total therefore settles.

**(b)** Writing $x^{-1/2}$ and integrating, $$\int_{1}^{t} x^{-1/2}\,dx = \left[2x^{1/2}\right]_{1}^{t} = 2\sqrt{t} - 2 \;(M1)(A1).$$

Here the partial area increases without limit as $t$ increases, because $2\sqrt{t} - 2$ does: extending the region to $t = 100$ gives an area of $18$, to $t = 10\,000$ an area of $198$, and to pass an area of $200$ the region must be taken out to $t = 10\,201$. There is no number that the area approaches from below, so the shaded region in the right-hand panel has no finite area (A1). The distinction between the two panels is therefore not that one region is longer than the other -- both are equally long -- but that one of them has a measurable area and the other does not.

**(c)** Both integrands are powers, $x^{-p}$, and both antiderivatives are powers, $x^{1-p}$ divided by $1-p$ (M1). What decides the outcome is the sign of the exponent $1 - p$ in the antiderivative. When $p > 1$ that exponent is negative, so the antiderivative is a negative power of $t$ and it tends to $0$ as $t$ grows; the area then settles at the finite value $\dfrac{1}{p-1}$, which for $p = 2$ is $1$, and for $p = 1.5$ would be $2$. When $p \leq 1$ the exponent is positive or zero, so the antiderivative grows with $t$ and there is no finite limit; for $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ it grows like $\sqrt{t}$ (A1). The property that decides, then, is how fast the integrand decays: a finite tail requires the integrand to fall away faster than $\dfrac{1}{x}$, and the two panels differ only in that their exponents are $2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$, one above the threshold and one below it.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for integrating $x^{-2}$ rather than $x^{2}$, or for any correct antiderivative of $x^{-2}$; (A1) for the evaluation $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$ with both limits used correctly; (A1) for the limit $1$, with the behaviour of $\dfrac{1}{t}$ stated. Three fields; credit two, and a candidate who writes down $1 - \dfrac{1}{t}$ and then states the area as $1$ without a word about the limit earns two of the three.

(b) (M1) for integrating $x^{-1/2}$; (A1) for $2\sqrt{t} - 2$; (A1) for the conclusion that the area is unbounded, with the reason that the expression grows without limit rather than settling. The conclusion is the mark that matters: an answer of '$\infty$' with no statement about the growth is worth the first two fields only.

(c) (M1) for comparing the antiderivatives of $x^{-p}$ and identifying the sign of $1 - p$ as the deciding feature; (A1) for expressing the criterion as $p > 1$, equivalently that the integrand must decay faster than $\dfrac{1}{x}$, and for observing that the two panels sit on opposite sides of that threshold. Do not accept a criterion stated in terms of the curves 'getting closer to the axis', since both of them do.
questions.explanation:
Two curves that both fall towards a horizontal axis, two regions that both run for ever, one area of exactly one and one area of nothing. The pair is the standard way into improper integrals and it is worth meeting as a picture before it is met as a definition, because the picture makes the surprise legible: nothing visible in the right-hand panel announces that its area is infinite, and nothing visible in the left-hand panel announces that its area is one.

The decision is made entirely by the antiderivative, and the antiderivative is made entirely by the exponent. Integrating $x^{-p}$ raises the power by one, so the behaviour at the upper limit is governed by whether $1 - p$ is negative or positive, which is the same question as whether $p$ is greater than one. This is why $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ is the standard example of a convergent tail and $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is the standard example of a divergent one: one sits just above the threshold and the other exactly on it. The right-hand panel here uses $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ rather than $p = 1$ on purpose, because $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ is visibly a different curve from $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ while $\dfrac{1}{x}$ would have invited the comparison with the logarithm, which is a separate story.

There is a temptation to reason from the width of the region, and it has to be resisted explicitly. Both regions are infinitely wide, so width cannot distinguish them; what distinguishes them is how quickly the height vanishes. A region of infinite width can have a finite area provided its height falls fast enough, and 'fast enough' has a sharp boundary in this family, at the inverse square root of nothing less convenient than the index one. The correct question is not how far the region extends but whether the area accumulated from $x = 1$ to $x = t$ approaches a limit as $t$ grows, and that question is answered by looking at the antiderivative rather than at the graph.

The same criterion recurs wherever a sum or an integral is taken over an infinite range, and the name for the case that fails is the same in each setting. Recognising $p > 1$ as the condition, and being able to produce the antiderivative that shows it, is the whole of the technique.

provenance.adaptation: Written for SL 5.11, extended by taking the limit of a definite integral as its upper bound grows. The two curves are 1/x^2 and 1/sqrt(x), chosen so that both antiderivatives are elementary and both limits can be read off directly, and so that the two exponents lie on opposite sides of the threshold at 1 without either of them being equal to 1. The figure places the two panels side by side at the same scale so that the comparison is between exponents rather than between pictures.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Observe that both shaded regions run to infinity to the right and conclude from their extent that neither has a finite area, since adding more of a region always adds more area to the total.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The extent of the region does not decide its area; the decay of the integrand does. Integrating x to the power minus p gives x to the power one minus p, so the behaviour at the upper limit is settled by the sign of that exponent, which means the area is finite exactly when p exceeds 1. The two panels differ only in that exponent, so one tail settles at 1 and the other grows without bound, and the limits have to be derived rather than read off the picture.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Both shaded regions are reported as having infinite area because both are infinitely wide, which leaves the left-hand tail described as infinite when its area is exactly 1, and it leaves the criterion for the two cases stated as the width of the region rather than as the exponent of the integrand.

verification.method: Both antiderivatives were checked by differentiating them back and by evaluating the definite integrals numerically at several upper limits. The left-hand tail was confirmed to approach 1 and the right-hand one to grow without limit, with the partial areas 18 at t = 100 and 198 at t = 10000 for the square-root curve, and the threshold for an area of 200 solved as t = 10201. The general finite-tail value 1/(p-1) was checked at p = 2, giving 1, and at p = 1.5, giving 2.
solution_skeleton: Integrate x to the power minus two from 1 to t and substitute the limits.
Let t grow and note that one over t tends to zero, so the partial area tends to one.
Integrate x to the power minus one half from 1 to t and substitute the limits.
Let t grow and note that two root t minus two grows without limit, so no finite area exists.
Compare the two antiderivatives as powers of t and identify the sign of the exponent as the deciding feature.
Express the criterion as the exponent p exceeding one and check that the two panels lie on opposite sides of it.
